claim: Invasive fungal infections cause 1.6 million deaths annually.
source: Invasive fungal infections cause 1.6 million deaths annually, primarily in immunocompromised individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Almeida et al., 2019; Bongomin et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2012) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Mortality rates from invasive fungal infections are as high as 90%.
source: Mortality rates are as high as 90% due to limited treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brown et al., 2012; Pianalto and Alspaugh, 2016; Scorzoni et al., 2017) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Fluconazole only inhibits growth instead of killing fungal cells.
source: The azole class antifungal, fluconazole, is widely available and has multi-species activity but only inhibits growth instead of killing fungal cells, necessitating long treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about fluconazole's fungistatic mechanism of action.

claim: The overlap2 method (O2M) identified 40 molecules that act synergistically with fluconazole.
source: We identified 40 molecules that act synergistically (amplify activity) and 19 molecules that act antagonistically (decrease efficacy) when combined with fluconazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput screening and validation assays described in the Results section.

claim: The overlap2 method (O2M) identified 19 molecules that act antagonistically with fluconazole.
source: We identified 40 molecules that act synergistically (amplify activity) and 19 molecules that act antagonistically (decrease efficacy) when combined with fluconazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput screening and validation assays described in the Results section.

claim: Critical frontline beta-lactam antibiotics antagonize fluconazole activity.
source: We found that critical frontline beta-lactam antibiotics antagonize fluconazole activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays testing beta-lactam antibiotics with fluconazole.

claim: Dicyclomine increases fungal cell permeability when combined with fluconazole.
source: A promising fluconazole-synergizing anticholinergic drug, dicyclomine, increases fungal cell permeability and inhibits nutrient intake when combined with fluconazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from propidium iodide internalization assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dicyclomine inhibits nutrient intake when combined with fluconazole.
source: A promising fluconazole-synergizing anticholinergic drug, dicyclomine, increases fungal cell permeability and inhibits nutrient intake when combined with fluconazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from toxic amino acid resistance assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dicyclomine and fluconazole combination doubled the time-to-endpoint of mice with Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis.
source: In vivo, this combination doubled the time-to-endpoint of mice with Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7.

claim: There are only four classes of antifungals.
source: To date, there are only four classes of antifungals, which primarily target the fungal cell envelope (cell wall and plasma membrane) (Coelho and Casadevall, 2016; Odds et al., 2003; Pianalto and Alspaugh, 2016; Scorzoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antifungals primarily target the fungal cell envelope (cell wall and plasma membrane).
source: To date, there are only four classes of antifungals, which primarily target the fungal cell envelope (cell wall and plasma membrane) (Coelho and Casadevall, 2016; Odds et al., 2003; Pianalto and Alspaugh, 2016; Scorzoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cryptococcosis causes 220,000 life-threatening infections annually worldwide.
source: Cryptococcosis is among the most common invasive mycoses, causing 220,000 life-threatening infections and 180,000 deaths annually worldwide (Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Rajasingham et al., 2017).

claim: Cryptococcosis causes 180,000 deaths annually worldwide.
source: Cryptococcosis is among the most common invasive mycoses, causing 220,000 life-threatening infections and 180,000 deaths annually worldwide (Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Rajasingham et al., 2017).

claim: Nearly 95% of cryptococcosis cases are caused by C. neoformans.
source: Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are the etiological agents of cryptococcosis, though nearly 95% of cases are caused by C. neoformans (Brown et al., 2012; Maziarz and Perfect, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brown et al., 2012; Maziarz and Perfect, 2016).

claim: Most individuals are exposed to C. neoformans by two years of age.
source: As C. neoformans is globally distributed throughout the environment, most individuals are exposed by two years of age (Goldman et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Goldman et al., 2001).

claim: HIV/AIDS patients account for 80% of cryptococcal cases.
source: Accordingly, HIV/AIDS patients account for 80% of cryptococcal cases (Maziarz and Perfect, 2016; Rajasingham et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Maziarz and Perfect, 2016; Rajasingham et al., 2017).

claim: 5-FC is unavailable in 78% of countries.
source: 5-FC is unavailable in 78% of countries, mostly due to licensing issues (Kneale et al., 2016; Mourad and Perfect, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kneale et al., 2016; Mourad and Perfect, 2018).

claim: Without the inclusion of 5-FC in the treatment regiment, mortality increases by up to 25%.
source: Without the inclusion of 5-FC in the treatment regiment, mortality increases by up to 25% (Kneale et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Kneale et al., 2016).

claim: Treatment with FLZ alone decreases survival rates from 75% to 30% in high burden areas.
source: Due to these therapeutic hurdles, many patients are treated with FLZ alone, which decreases survival rates from 75% to 30% in high burden areas (Kneale et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Kneale et al., 2016).

claim: Synergistic interactions occur when the combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of each drug's individual activity.
source: Synergistic interactions occur when the combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of each drug's individual activity (Cokol et al., 2011; Kalan and Wright, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cokol et al., 2011; Kalan and Wright, 2011).

claim: Amphotericin B and 5-FC act synergistically.
source: In addition, Amphotericin B and 5-FC act synergistically, and mortality rates increase dramatically when one is unavailable (Beggs, 1986; Kneale et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Beggs, 1986; Kneale et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2006).

claim: Mortality rates increase dramatically when either Amphotericin B or 5-FC is unavailable.
source: In addition, Amphotericin B and 5-FC act synergistically, and mortality rates increase dramatically when one is unavailable (Beggs, 1986; Kneale et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Beggs, 1986; Kneale et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2006).

claim: 56% of AIDS patients experience polypharmacy.
source: 56% of AIDS patients experience polypharmacy, or greater than five medications (Siefried et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Siefried et al., 2018).

claim: Polypharmacy doubles the risk of antiviral therapy nonadherence to 49% of HIV+ patients.
source: Polypharmacy doubles the risk of antiviral therapy nonadherence to 49% of HIV+ patients (Lohman et al., 2018) and increases mortality by 68% in HIV+ and 99% in HIV- patients (Cantudo-Cuenca et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Lohman et al., 2018).

claim: Polypharmacy increases mortality by 68% in HIV+ patients.
source: Polypharmacy doubles the risk of antiviral therapy nonadherence to 49% of HIV+ patients (Lohman et al., 2018) and increases mortality by 68% in HIV+ and 99% in HIV- patients (Cantudo-Cuenca et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cantudo-Cuenca et al., 2014).

claim: Polypharmacy increases mortality by 99% in HIV- patients.
source: Polypharmacy doubles the risk of antiviral therapy nonadherence to 49% of HIV+ patients (Lohman et al., 2018) and increases mortality by 68% in HIV+ and 99% in HIV- patients (Cantudo-Cuenca et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cantudo-Cuenca et al., 2014).

claim: The O2M method uses synergy prediction mutants to identify molecules that interact with fluconazole.
source: Using these synergy prediction mutants, we identified 313 putative FLZ synergistic molecules (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput screen described in the Results section.

claim: 31% of molecules predicted by O2M to synergize with FLZ were correctly predicted.
source: We found that 40 molecules were synergistic with FLZ, meaning 31% of these molecules were correctly predicted by O2M (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays validating the O2M predictions.

claim: 46% of predicted interactions were validated by checkerboard assay to truly interact with FLZ.
source: Of the predicted interactions, 46% were validated by checkerboard assay to truly interact with FLZ (synergistic or antagonistic) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays and is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 75% of structurally similar molecules acted synergistically with FLZ.
source: Overall, 75% of the structurally similar molecules acted synergistically with FLZ, demonstrating that structure can serve as a powerful basis to predict additional synergistic combinations prior to elucidating mechanism of action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays testing structurally similar molecules.

claim: Structural similarity can predict additional synergistic combinations.
source: Overall, 75% of the structurally similar molecules acted synergistically with FLZ, demonstrating that structure can serve as a powerful basis to predict additional synergistic combinations prior to elucidating mechanism of action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that structurally similar molecules have similar synergistic interactions with FLZ.

claim: Sertraline hydrochloride synergistically inhibited the growth of most C. neoformans strains and fungal species tested.
source: Of the FLZ-interacting pairs, sertraline hydrochloride (HCl), clomipramine HCl, benzalkonium chloride, berbamine HCl and dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most of the strains/species (Figure 4A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Clomipramine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most C. neoformans strains and fungal species tested.
source: Of the FLZ-interacting pairs, sertraline hydrochloride (HCl), clomipramine HCl, benzalkonium chloride, berbamine HCl and dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most of the strains/species (Figure 4A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Benzalkonium chloride synergistically inhibited the growth of most C. neoformans strains and fungal species tested.
source: Of the FLZ-interacting pairs, sertraline hydrochloride (HCl), clomipramine HCl, benzalkonium chloride, berbamine HCl and dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most of the strains/species (Figure 4A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Berbamine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most C. neoformans strains and fungal species tested.
source: Of the FLZ-interacting pairs, sertraline hydrochloride (HCl), clomipramine HCl, benzalkonium chloride, berbamine HCl and dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most of the strains/species (Figure 4A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most C. neoformans strains and fungal species tested.
source: Of the FLZ-interacting pairs, sertraline hydrochloride (HCl), clomipramine HCl, benzalkonium chloride, berbamine HCl and dicyclomine HCl synergistically inhibited the growth of most of the strains/species (Figure 4A,B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nafcillin sodium was antagonistic with FLZ in most of the strains/species tested.
source: Nafcillin sodium was antagonistic with FLZ in most of the strains/species (Figure 4M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays across multiple strains and species, shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Nafcillin is a common penicillinase-resistant penicillin antibiotic.
source: Nafcillin is a common penicillinase-resistant penicillin antibiotic (Letourneau, 2019; Nathwani and Wood, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Letourneau, 2019; Nathwani and Wood, 1993).

claim: Nafcillin antagonized FLZ activity in all 7 FLZ-resistant C. neoformans strains tested.
source: In all 7 C. neoformans strains, nafcillin antagonized FLZ activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays on FLZ-resistant strains.

claim: Oxacillin antagonizes FLZ.
source: Antagonism with FLZ was not a universal attribute among penicillin antibiotics but was evident for oxacillin and methicillin (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Methicillin antagonizes FLZ.
source: Antagonism with FLZ was not a universal attribute among penicillin antibiotics but was evident for oxacillin and methicillin (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Cefazolin antagonizes FLZ.
source: We also tested a first-generation cephalosporin, cefazolin, that is often prescribed in place of nafcillin (Letourneau, 2019; Miller et al., 2018) and a second-generation cephalosporin, cefonicid. We found that both of these molecules also antagonize FLZ (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Cefonicid antagonizes FLZ.
source: We also tested a first-generation cephalosporin, cefazolin, that is often prescribed in place of nafcillin (Letourneau, 2019; Miller et al., 2018) and a second-generation cephalosporin, cefonicid. We found that both of these molecules also antagonize FLZ (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Vancomycin does not interact with FLZ.
source: These included vancomycin and linezolid (Fowler and Holland, 2018; Lowy, 2019), neither of which interacted with FLZ (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Linezolid does not interact with FLZ.
source: These included vancomycin and linezolid (Fowler and Holland, 2018; Lowy, 2019), neither of which interacted with FLZ (Figure 5M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Nafcillin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes in humans.
source: In particular, nafcillin antagonizes warfarin and other drugs in vivo by inducing cytochrome P450 enzymes through an unknown mechanism, which increases warfarin metabolism (King et al., 2018; Wungwattana and Savic, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (King et al., 2018; Wungwattana and Savic, 2017).

claim: FLZ inhibits 14α-demethylase, a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme.
source: FLZ inhibits a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme, 14α-demethylase, which halts ergosterol biosynthesis and fungal growth (Figure 5N; Odds et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Odds et al., 2003) and is illustrated in Figure 5N.

claim: High-dose nafcillin treatment increases ergosterol levels in C. neoformans.
source: We found an increase in ergosterol with a high-dose nafcillin treatment (Figure 5O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sterol extraction and metabolomics analysis shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Amphotericin B was synergistic with nafcillin.
source: Indeed, amphotericin B was synergistic with nafcillin in checkerboard assays giving an average FICI score of 0.5 (Figure 5—source data 2), further suggesting that nafcillin increases ergosterol levels in C. neoformans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays.

claim: Nafcillin antagonizes ketoconazole activity.
source: We found that nafcillin also antagonizes ketoconazole activity, producing an average FICI score of 5 against C. neoformans (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays.

claim: Dicyclomine is an FDA-approved drug used to treat urinary incontinence.
source: Dicyclomine is an FDA-approved drug, also known as Bentyl, used to treat urinary incontinence (Malone and Okano, 1999; Page and Dirnberger, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Malone and Okano, 1999; Page and Dirnberger, 1981).

claim: Dicyclomine targets a G-protein coupled receptor encoded by the CHRM1 gene.
source: It targets a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) encoded by the CHRM1 gene (UniProt Consortium., 2018; Kilbinger and Stein, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (UniProt Consortium., 2018; Kilbinger and Stein, 1988).

claim: C. neoformans does not have a CHRM1 ortholog.
source: C. neoformans does not have a CHRM1 ortholog, but there are a large number of GPCRs in fungi that could be potential targets (Xue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Xue et al., 2008) and inference from genomic data.

claim: 44% of annotated dicyclomine-resistant mutants were involved in transport and trafficking.
source: When we screened a deletion library of C. neoformans for mutants resistant to dicyclomine, we found that 44% of the annotated dicyclomine-resistant mutants were involved in transport and trafficking, suggesting that those processes may be related to dicyclomine's mechanism (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the dicyclomine resistance screen shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Dicyclomine permeabilizes fungal cells at high doses.
source: Using propidium iodide internalization as a measure of cell permeability, we observed that dicyclomine, similar to FLZ, permeabilizes fungal cells at high doses (Figure 6C,D,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from propidium iodide internalization assays shown in Figure 6C, D, F, and G.

claim: Low concentrations of dicyclomine and FLZ in combination cause a greater than additive increase in cell permeability.
source: Furthermore, we saw a greater than additive increase in permeability when fungal cells were treated with low concentrations of dicyclomine and FLZ in combination (Figure 6E and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from propidium iodide internalization assays shown in Figure 6E and H.

claim: Dicyclomine + FLZ combination is fungicidal.
source: Thus, our synergistic combination is fungicidal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fungicidal assay shown in Figure 6M and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dicyclomine was synergistic with FLZ against each FLZ-resistant strain and species tested.
source: Dicyclomine was synergistic with FLZ against each of these resistant strains and species (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays on FLZ-resistant strains shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dicyclomine + ketoconazole combination was synergistic.
source: We found the dicyclomine + ketoconazole combination was also synergistic in a checkerboard assay, giving an average FICI score of 0.313 (Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from checkerboard assays.

claim: Dicyclomine is orally bioavailable.
source: Dicyclomine is orally bioavailable and able to cross the blood brain barrier (Das et al., 2013; Koerselman et al., 1999), which makes it particularly promising for fungal meningitis treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Das et al., 2013; Koerselman et al., 1999).

claim: Dicyclomine is able to cross the blood brain barrier.
source: Dicyclomine is orally bioavailable and able to cross the blood brain barrier (Das et al., 2013; Koerselman et al., 1999), which makes it particularly promising for fungal meningitis treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Das et al., 2013; Koerselman et al., 1999).

claim: At 8 days post-inoculation, 100% of mice exhibited fungal dissemination to the liver.
source: Colony forming unit data indicated that at this point 100% of the mice exhibited fungal dissemination to the liver, and 40% exhibited dissemination to the brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 8 days post-inoculation, 40% of mice exhibited fungal dissemination to the brain.
source: Colony forming unit data indicated that at this point 100% of the mice exhibited fungal dissemination to the liver, and 40% exhibited dissemination to the brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dicyclomine alone did not affect mouse survival compared to PBS-treatment.
source: Dicyclomine alone did not affect mouse survival compared to PBS-treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dicyclomine in combination with FLZ significantly improved survival over FLZ alone in a dose-dependent manner.
source: However, dicyclomine in combination with FLZ significantly improved survival over FLZ alone in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7), indicating that dicyclomine is not effective at treating cryptococcosis on its own, but could well be of therapeutic benefit when combined with FLZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7.

claim: O2M's synergy prediction genes tend to identify synergizers with mechanism of action functionally related to those of the starting synergizer.
source: This work and our application of O2M to antibiotic trimethoprim (Wambaugh et al., 2017) suggests that O2M's synergy prediction genes tend to identify synergizers with mechanism of action functionally related to those of the starting synergizer.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current work and previous application of O2M to trimethoprim (Wambaugh et al., 2017).

claim: Sertraline inhibits phospholipase activity in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Here, one of the known synergizers used to identify synergy prediction genes, sertraline, inhibits phospholipase activity in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which inhibits vesicle formation Rainey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Rainey et al., 2010).

claim: Of the 59 FLZ interacting molecules identified, 10 have been previously described in various fungi.
source: Of the 59 FLZ interacting molecules we identified, 10 have been previously described in various fungi.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with published literature.

claim: Nafcillin can reach mean plasma concentrations in humans of 30 µg/mL after a single 500 mg dose.
source: Nafcillin can reach mean plasma concentrations in humans of 30 µg/mL after a single 500 mg dose (FDA, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to FDA documentation (FDA, 2020).

claim: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of drug metabolism due to elevation of hepatic cytochrome P450 through increased gene expression.
source: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of drug metabolism due to elevation of hepatic cytochrome P450 through increased gene expression (Bolt, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bolt, 2004).

claim: The combination of rifampicin and FLZ lowered the levels of FLZ.
source: This combination did indeed lower the levels of FLZ (Panomvana Na Ayudhya et al., 2004), resulting in relapse of cryptococcal meningitis (Coker et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Panomvana Na Ayudhya et al., 2004).

claim: The combination of rifampicin and FLZ resulted in relapse of cryptococcal meningitis.
source: This combination did indeed lower the levels of FLZ (Panomvana Na Ayudhya et al., 2004), resulting in relapse of cryptococcal meningitis (Coker et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Coker et al., 1990).

claim: In a recent autopsy study, 10 of 16 patients who died of cryptococcosis were administered either a penicillin or a cephalosporin.
source: In a recent autopsy study, 10 or 16 patients who died of cryptococcosis were administered either a penicillin or a cephalosporin (Hurtado et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hurtado et al., 2019).

claim: Dicyclomine's serum concentration in mice administered 60 µg was 0.2–0.6 µg/mL at 18 hr post injection.
source: Dicyclomine's serum concentration in mice administered 60 µg was 0.2–0.6 µg/mL at 18 hr post injection (Karaka et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Karaka et al., 2004).

claim: Dicyclomine improves mouse survival when combined with FLZ even at low doses.
source: While this is lower than dicyclomine's antifungal MIC, dicyclomine improves mouse survival when combined with FLZ even at these low doses (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the murine infection model shown in Figure 7.

claim: Nafcillin may induce cytochrome P450 enzymes in C. neoformans, counteracting FLZ's mechanism of action.
source: We hypothesized that nafcillin may also induce cytochrome P450 enzymes, such as 14α-demethylase, in C. neoformans, counteracting FLZ's mechanism of action.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from nafcillin's known effects in humans and the observed antagonism with FLZ.

claim: The combination of dicyclomine and FLZ phenocopies the effect of simultaneously inhibiting Golgi trafficking and blocking ergosterol synthesis.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, simultaneously inhibiting Golgi trafficking and blocking ergosterol synthesis leads to mislocalization of essential plasma membrane transporters (Estrada et al., 2015). We hypothesized that the combination of dicyclomine and FLZ will phenocopy this effect in C. neoformans (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from published work in S. cerevisiae (Estrada et al., 2015) and the observed effects of dicyclomine and FLZ.

claim: Certain amino acid transporters' function is decreased and may be mislocalized when cells are treated with dicyclomine + FLZ.
source: This demonstrates that certain amino acid transporters' function is decreased and they thus may be mislocalized, conferring resistance to toxic forms of tryptophan.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the toxic amino acid resistance assay data shown in Figure 6I-L.

claim: Synergistic interactions can cause fungistatic drugs to switch to fungicidal.
source: Synergistic interactions can also cause fungistatic drugs to switch to fungicidal, providing a more effective treatment option (Cowen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Cowen et al., 2009).

claim: FLZ is fungistatic.
source: FLZ is fungistatic, inhibiting the growth the C. neoformans cells but not killing them (Hazen, 1998; Klepser et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hazen, 1998; Klepser et al., 1998).

claim: Amphotericin B is fungicidal.
source: As a control, we tested the fungicidal drug amphotericin B (Gray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gray et al., 2012).

claim: After 9 hr of treatment, C. neoformans cells treated with all synergistic combinations and doses of FLZ 1/3 MIC and higher exhibited increased cell death.
source: After 9 hr of treatment, we found that C. neoformans cells treated with all synergistic combinations and doses of FLZ 1/3 MIC and higher exhibited increased cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fungicidal assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2J.

claim: After 24 hr of treatment, all synergistic combinations exhibited nearly 100% cell death.
source: After 24 hr of treatment, all synergistic combinations exhibited nearly 100% cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fungicidal assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2K.

claim: The combination with the lowest FLZ + dicyclomine doses had significantly more cell death than untreated or single agent-treated cells after 9- and 24 hr treatment.
source: When evaluating the combination with the lowest FLZ + dicyclomine doses, we did not observe cell death at 3 hr. However, after 9- and 24 hr treatment, the combination had significantly more cell death than untreated or single agent-treated cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2M; Figure 6M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fungicidal assay shown in Figure 6M and Figure 6—figure supplement 2M.

claim: Amphotericin B kills C. neoformans cells by binding and extracting ergosterol from the plasma membrane.
source: Since amphotericin B kills target cells by binding and extracting ergosterol from the plasma membrane (Anderson et al., 2014), we hypothesized that if nafcillin increases ergosterol levels in C. neoformans, nafcillin would act synergistically with amphotericin B by increasing amphotericin B binding sites (i.e. ergosterol).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Anderson et al., 2014).

claim: Ketoconazole inhibits ergosterol synthesis.
source: Lastly, ketoconazole is an imidazole antifungal that, like fluconazole, inhibits ergosterol synthesis (Marichal et al., 1985; Odds et al., 2003) and is also a potent inhibitor of antiretroviral drug metabolism through its inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes (Dooley et al., 2008; Kaeser et al., 2009; Polk et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Marichal et al., 1985; Odds et al., 2003).

claim: Ketoconazole is a potent inhibitor of antiretroviral drug metabolism through its inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes.
source: Lastly, ketoconazole is an imidazole antifungal that, like fluconazole, inhibits ergosterol synthesis (Marichal et al., 1985; Odds et al., 2003) and is also a potent inhibitor of antiretroviral drug metabolism through its inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes (Dooley et al., 2008; Kaeser et al., 2009; Polk et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dooley et al., 2008; Kaeser et al., 2009; Polk et al., 1999).

claim: Ketoconazole is used in certain areas worldwide to increase the half-life of antivirals in blood.
source: Ketoconazole is used in certain areas worldwide in order to increase the half-life of antivirals in blood (Dooley et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dooley et al., 2008).

claim: The O2M screen predicted that 16% of the library's small molecules would interact with FLZ.
source: Overall, the O2M screen predicted that 16% of the library's small molecules would interact with FLZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the high-throughput screen shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CNAG 00573 encodes a NADH dehydrogenase.
source: CNAG 00573 encodes a NADH dehydrogenase (Janbon et al., 2014), CNAG 03664 encodes NIC1, a high-affinity nickel-transporter (Singh et al., 2013), and CNAG 03917 encodes a nuclear pore complex protein homologous to Nup75 (Liu et al., 2008; Stajich et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Janbon et al., 2014).

claim: The O2M screen identified 313 putative FLZ synergistic molecules.
source: Using these synergy prediction mutants, we identified 313 putative FLZ synergistic molecules (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput screen.

claim: Synergistic interactions are defined as a ≥ 4 fold decrease in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of each small molecule in the pair, resulting in a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) of ≤0.5.
source: Synergistic interactions are defined as a ≥ 4 fold decrease in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of each small molecule in the pair, resulting in a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) of ≤0.5 (Johnson et al., 2004; Odds, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature defining synergy (Johnson et al., 2004; Odds, 2003).

claim: Antagonistic interactions are defined by a minimum 4-fold increase in MICs causing increased fungal growth and a FICI ≥4.
source: These interactions are defined by a minimum 4-fold increase in MICs causing increased fungal growth and a FICI ≥4 (Cetin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature defining antagonism (Cetin et al., 2013).
